No converse is claimed: the negative symmetry statement is proved by a single exhibited counterexample, and no if-and-only-if appears.

citations.quote:
There is an explicit semi-infinite wedge bar $\psi$ with the vacuum fixed,
coefficient bar $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $U_q$/bar compatibility, whose restriction
to $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ is the normalized highest module bar. On **all** partitions
its integral triangular correction is

$$G(\lambda)=|\lambda\rangle+\sum_{\mu\ \text{strictly dominated by}\ \lambda}d_{\mu,\lambda}(q)|\mu\rangle, \qquad d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q],$$

with diagonal $1$ and same $e$-core support; the family $\{G(\lambda)\}$ is an
$A$-basis of $F_A$ and an $A_0$-basis of $F_0$, with the actual infinity chart
and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form
the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis
suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other
field irreducible summands. The transpose equality
$d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ is **false** in general; the source symmetry
concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use
$(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients require the restricted Gram
inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

A partition is **regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity $<e$,
and **restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$. Conjugation
$C:\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is the comparison map between the regular and the
restricted models; it sends the residue $i$ to $-i$. It is **not** the
same-model sign involution.

On the regular basic crystal of
[[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]] define
$M$ by negating all colors of a lowering path from the empty partition:
$M(f_ib)=f_{-i}M(b)$ for every edge, $M(\varnothing)=\varnothing$. The
restricted sign involution is the conjugate $CMC^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: The degrees $\le3$. Solving the triangular bar equations degree by degree with the reversal bar: in degree $2$ the only correction of $2$ is $q\,11$; in degree $3$ the partition $21$ is the only shape whose residue multiset forces no correction and $3$ receives the correction $q\,111$; the remaining shapes are bar-fixed. This gives the displayed degree-$\le3$ elements, and the basic labels are the $2$-regular ones, namely $\varnothing,1,2,3,21$, with $11$ and $111$ non-regular.

The degree-$4$ matrix. Repeating the finite bar recursion in degree $4$ gives the displayed five columns: the columns are $G(4)=|4\rangle+q|31\rangle+q|211\rangle+q^2|1111\rangle$, $G(31)=|31\rangle+q|22\rangle+q^2|211\rangle$, $G(22)=|22\rangle+q|211\rangle$, $G(211)=|211\rangle+q|1111\rangle$ and $G(1111)=|1111\rangle$, and the matrix is unitriangular with diagonal $1$; the basic columns are the regular labels $4$ and $31$. Every entry lies in $\mathbb Z[q]$ by [F1], and the dominance support is visible from the positions of the nonzero entries.

The false transpose symmetry. Conjugation of partitions sends $211\mapsto31$ and $4\mapsto1111$, so the transpose-conjugation equality would require $d_{(211),(4)}=d_{(1111),(31)}$; but the degree-$4$ matrix gives $d_{(211),(4)}=q$ and $d_{(1111),(31)}=0$. Hence the equality fails in general; the source's symmetry statement concerns the bar transition matrix $A$, not the lower matrix $D$.

Conclusion. The displayed elements are the actual lower global basis elements in degrees $\le4$, their coefficients are integral and dominance-triangular, the basic columns are the regular labels, and the naive transpose symmetry of $D$ is refuted by the explicit pair.
